stymie

/STY-mee/ - the stress falls on STY · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Stymie means to block the progress of an effort so completely that it stalls, leaving no clear way forward.

The detectives were stymied for weeks: the vault had been emptied, yet every lock was still sealed from the inside, and each new lead went nowhere.

Example

The city's plan to uncover the buried creek was stymied by a single missing utility map — until it turned up, no crew could dig an inch without risking the gas lines that ran somewhere beneath the park.

Stymie says more than 'slowed' and less than 'defeated': a stymied effort is not destroyed, it is stuck — halted at a standstill until something changes. The missing map does not doom the creek project or merely delay it; it freezes the work in place, with the goal still visible and no safe way to move toward it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

obstruct: To obstruct is to place a barrier in the way — a road, a view, or a process can all be obstructed, and the word describes the barrier, not the outcome. Stymie reports the result: the effort has actually stalled, stuck with no clear way forward until something changes.

baffle: To baffle is to defeat the mind — a baffled person cannot understand what they face. Stymie defeats the effort itself: a stymied team may see the obstacle with perfect clarity and still be unable to get past it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

facilitate: to make a process easier and help it move ahead

advance: to push a plan or effort forward

Where it sits · how completely the obstacle stops the effort

hinder → stymie → thwart

hinder vs. stymie: Hinder is milder than stymie: a hindered effort is slowed — detours, setbacks, lost time — but it still inches forward, while a stymied one has stopped dead with no way ahead.

thwart vs. stymie: Thwart is stronger than stymie: a stymied plan is stuck and can still revive if the obstacle clears, while a thwarted plan has been defeated outright — that attempt is finished.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stymie: the whole word is the root — a Scots golf term for a ball blocking another's line to the hole (deeper origin unknown)

Put it together: Stymie has no prefix or suffix to peel apart — the whole word is the root. It entered English through nineteenth-century Scottish golf, where a stymie was an opponent's ball sitting squarely between your ball and the cup: the hole is still there, but the line to it is blocked. Golf abolished the stymie rule in the 1950s, yet by then the verb had escaped the course, and anything that leaves an effort blocked in mid-course can stymie it. Where the Scots got the word is genuinely unknown — perhaps from stime, 'a glimpse' — so the trail honestly stops there.

The form you will actually meet: stymied: On the green, a player was stymied when an opponent's ball lay dead in her line; today the passive form is everywhere — negotiators are stymied by a veto, researchers are stymied by missing records — and it is the shape of the word you will most often meet on the page.

Strength Check

Word Choice

vivid and slightly informal; at home in news reporting

Stymie is the newsroom's word for gridlock: bills are stymied in committee, mergers are stymied by regulators, and the word usually arrives in the passive — plans are stymied by something. This unit hands you its nearest neighbors, and they divide the work cleanly: hinder only slows an effort that keeps moving, and forestall stops trouble before it ever starts, while stymie catches the effort already underway that has run into a wall and stalled. In formal prose, 'obstruct' or 'block' will do; stymie adds the golfer's exasperation — so near the hole, and no way through.
